nameStory: The gold-striped leaftier moth gets its name from the shimmering golden stripes that decorate its wings and its caterpillars' habit of creating leaf shelters. The larvae are master architects, rolling or tying leaves together to form tent-like hideaways where they feed and develop. In fact, the scientific name 'tentoriferella' comes from the Latin word for tent, celebrating this clever construction behavior.
description: The gold-striped leaftier moth is a small, slender moth with distinctive golden stripes running along its narrow wings. These delicate moths have a wingspan of about an inch (20-26 mm), making them roughly the size of a large thumbnail. When at rest, they hold their wings close to their body, giving them an elongated, streamlined appearance. They belong to the flat-bodied moth family, which means they can squeeze into surprisingly tight spaces.

idTips.label: Golden wing stripes
idTips.description: Look for bright golden or yellowish stripes running lengthwise along the wings, which catch the light beautifully and shimmer when the moth moves

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: About thumbnail-sized with wings spanning just under an inch, much smaller than the common moths that flutter around porch lights

idTips.label: Narrow wing shape
idTips.description: Wings are distinctly long and slender rather than broad, giving the moth a sleek, torpedo-like silhouette when folded

idTips.label: Fall timing
idTips.description: Active during September and October when most other moths have disappeared for the season

idTips.label: Flat-bodied profile
idTips.description: When resting against bark or walls, the moth appears remarkably thin and pressed flat, almost two-dimensional

idTips.label: Leaf-tied caterpillar shelters
idTips.description: Look for leaves that have been rolled or tied together on ash, oak, maple, and other deciduous trees - signs of the larvae at work

habitat: Gold-striped leaftier moths are found wherever their host trees grow, particularly in mixed deciduous forests and woodland edges throughout New England. They're especially common in areas with white ash and black ash trees, but also frequent maple-oak forests, suburban areas with mature shade trees, and parks with diverse tree plantings. Look for them around outdoor lights near wooded areas during their brief fall flight period.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not active; overwintering pupae are developing inside cocoons hidden in leaf litter or bark crevices.
seasonality.summer: Eggs hatch and tiny caterpillars begin creating their characteristic leaf shelters, though the larvae are well-hidden inside their rolled leaf homes.
seasonality.fall: Adult moths emerge and are most active from September through October, when you'll see them attracted to lights on warm evenings.
seasonality.winter: Adults have died off and the next generation overwinters as pupae, waiting for spring warmth to continue their development cycle.

funFact: These caterpillars are incredibly picky interior designers - they don't just roll any old leaf, but carefully select the perfect leaves and then use silk to stitch them together with the precision of tiny tailors, creating custom-fitted homes that protect them from both predators and weather.
confusionNotes: The golden stripes make this moth fairly distinctive among New England's fall-flying moths, though other small moths might appear similar at first glance. Remember the timing - most moths fly earlier in the season, so a small moth with golden markings in September or October is likely your gold-striped leaftier.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'leaftier,' these moths don't actually tie leaves in the way we might imagine with string or rope - instead, the caterpillars use silk they produce from their bodies to bind leaf edges together, much like a spider uses silk to build webs.
compareHints: This is the only Machimia species commonly found in New England, making identification easier within its genus. Compared to other flat-bodied moths in the Depressariidae family, the gold-striped leaftier is distinguished by its prominent golden wing stripes and relatively late fall flight period. Most similar moths in this family lack the distinctive metallic golden markings and fly earlier in the season.
